1.pericope_label: Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up... In God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me

schools.summary: Reads the heading as musical and philological data. The plural in the title is taken as distant men or distant places, the vowel-pointing is questioned, a proposed rendering is rejected on lexical grounds in favour of dove of the distant terebinths, and the preposition is construed as after the tune of rather than concerning. On the opening plea the same approach parses the word for man as either mortal man or contemptuously a rabble, finds the root behind swallow up unclear, and denies that the closing phrase of the second verse addresses God at all, taking it as an adverbial accusative meaning proudly.

Anchors the psalm in the flight to Achish. David, driven from every hiding place, was apprehended and escaped by feigning madness; the psalm proves faith was secretly in exercise even under that weakness, and records a strenuous contest between faith and fear. The plea itself is grounded in the danger of Goliath's own city, where nothing could be expected from men whose tender mercies are cruel, so that no merit is pleaded but mercy alone.

Canvasses the ancient versions on the title and offers a construction that makes it a prayer for the psalmist and the oppressed band that shared his misfortunes in distant places, then dismisses the whole enterprise as conjecture not worth an hour's labour. Reads the disputed phrase in the second verse as from on high, that is, from the place of authority, and takes praising his word as praising God through God's own help.

Keeps the dove as a portrait of the psalmist: innocent, driven from the sanctuary, mourning in distant countries yet silent, and so a type of Christ dumb before the shearers and a pattern for Christians. Itemises the complaint as many, barbarous, unanimous and subtle enemies, and presses the plea for mercy as a claim on the tenderest attribute: if justice has let loose the enemies, let mercy shorten their chain. Fear is allowed to stand alongside faith, since it is a blessed fear that drives a man to trust.

Treats the inscription as a doorway to be read before entering. At the end means Christ, since the end of the law is Christ for righteousness, and the people put far off from holy men are identified by another title altogether, the one written over the cross in three tongues and so confirmed as by three witnesses.

debates.question: What is the psalm's heading, and does it repay study at all?

positions.summary: A biographical and devotional notice: the dove is David himself, or the oppressed band with him, in flight and in exile.
A musical and philological datum naming a tune, to be settled by lexicon and pointing rather than by biography.
Worthless conjecture; none of the titles in the book is worth an hour's labour.
A figure to be read spiritually, pointing through David to Christ and to the title fixed over the cross.

debates.question: Does the close of the second verse address God as most High?

positions.summary: No: the word is an adverbial accusative meaning proudly, describing how the enemies fight.
No: it means from on high, naming the elevated place of authority from which the attack is directed.
Yes: it is a vocative, and the plea is lodged with the Most High against numbers too great for the sufferer.

outliers.reading: Reads the heading itself as the psalm's subject, identifying the people put far off with those named in the inscription over the cross, so that the title of the psalm and the title of the crucifixion interpret one another.

themes: Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up; he fighting daily oppresseth me.
Mine enemies would daily swallow me up: for they be many that fight against me, O thou most High.
What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me.

5.pericope_label: Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil... put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?

schools.summary: Works the vocabulary. The verb behind wrest properly means afflict, so injure my cause is defensible; hiding themselves is better rendered they set spies, and marking his steps is literally watching his heels. The opening of the seventh verse is judged unclear in the received text and the ancient versions no help, sense being gained only by a slight emendation yielding for iniquity thou wilt requite them. On the counted wanderings the school divides internally between a singular sense of mental restlessness and an insistence that what is numbered is the measurable life of a fugitive rather than flight in the abstract.

Derives the verb for wresting from the shaping of the human body and applies it to speech forced into a shape it never had, noting a second sense in which the psalmist's own words cause grief. Rules out reading the wanderings as sins, since of those God keeps no account at all, and takes them as the recorded flights of a man hunted like a partridge on the mountains.

Reads the persecution as political intelligence work: spies collecting the psalmist's sayings and twisting them by innuendo into treason, cabals dressed as concern for the safety of the state, and lurking watchers prying into private actions. Objects that the translators have mistaken the word rendered soul, which means animal life rather than the immortal spirit. Hears in the bottle an allusion to the ancient lachrymatories in which tears for the dead were gathered and offered at the tomb.

Generalises the malice into a law of persecution: a wolf can always find in a lamb's discourse a reason for eating him, and prayers are blasphemies read the wrong way upwards. Cowards gather for odds, and men of malice are men of cowardice. On the counted steps and bottled tears the emphasis falls on divine attention — every weary step numbered, the tears sealed among God's treasures, and God not casting from his care those whom men have cast out.

debates.question: What are the wanderings that God counts?

positions.summary: Outward flights from place to place under pursuit, numbered as literal removes.
Inward restlessness — the tossings to and fro of the mind — read in the singular and parallel to the tears.
Neither flight in the abstract nor mood, but the unsettled life of a fugitive, numerable by its duration and its many temporary stays.

debates.question: Does the bottle allude to the ancient custom of collecting tears in phials?

positions.summary: Yes, and the custom is described in detail from surviving examples in glass, pottery and agate.
No: the point is a wordplay between the words for bottle and wandering, and the phials must not be imported.
No: the metaphor is robuster than any fashionable phial, since a leathern bottle would scarce hold such floods.

outliers.reading: Interrupts the exposition to charge the translators with mistaking the word rendered soul more than any other word in either Testament, insisting it denotes animal life rather than the immortal spirit.

themes: Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil.
They gather themselves together, they hide themselves, they mark my steps, when they wait for my soul.
Shall they escape by iniquity? in thine anger cast down the people, O God.
Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?

9.pericope_label: When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies turn back... that I may walk before God in the light of the living?

schools.summary: Restricts itself to the wording. The phrase behind thy vows, meaning vows made to thee, is flagged as a most unusual form; the closing clause is preferred in the perfect, hast thou not delivered, rather than the received future; and the word behind falling is noted as literally a thrust. Alongside this the vow language is parsed as incumbent upon me, with the pledged vow-offering distinguished from the thank-offering and neither allowed to be wanting.

Takes the repetition of the refrain as deliberate, doubled for the greater certainty of the thing and to show a fixed resolution. Reads the vows as debts contracted in distress and now to be paid, fresh in the memory at the very point where men commonly forget. On the final verse objects that the soul cannot die, being immortal, so that the rescue must be of the person from imminent danger, then widens it to the spiritual death from which grace quickens and the eternal death over which the second death has no power.

Makes the cry itself the turning point: the moment the enemies know God is being called on, they take flight, a certainty grounded in repeated experience of divine interposition rather than in argument. Turns the vows on the reader, listing the renunciations every believer has already promised and asking whether he will pay them, and reads the last verse as preservation from any false way and a steadying in the godly course.

Holds the refrain's ambiguity open — whether the praising is done by God's grace or directed at God's word and its faithfulness — and draws from it the rule that praise never special in its direction cannot be very thoughtful. Refuses to hear the vows as a weight: not a burden but a badge, not fetters but a bridle, with God not merely witness to them but party. Allows the closing words to be prayer pleading experience or praise raising expectation, since God has done the greater and will therefore do the less.

debates.question: Is the final clause a petition still outstanding or a deliverance already granted?

positions.summary: Already granted: read the verb as a perfect, hast thou not delivered.
Still outstanding, and confidently expected — the greater deliverance already given is the pledge of the lesser still to come.
Deliberately both: the words serve as prayer pleading experience and as praise raising expectation, and faith may thank God for mercies in prospect as well as in possession.

debates.question: What does praising his word in God mean?

positions.summary: The word is the object of praise: God is praised for the promise and for the faithfulness with which he keeps it.
God is the means: by his grace and help the praise is offered, so that even the emotion directed to him is produced by him.
Both senses stand, and the ambiguity itself teaches that praise should be specific in its direction.

outliers.reading: Blocks the plain sense of the deliverance on doctrinal grounds — the soul cannot die, being immortal — and so reads soul as person, before extending the rescue outward to spiritual and eternal death.

themes: When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies turn back: this I know; for God is for me.
In God will I praise his word: in the Lord will I praise his word.
In God have I put my trust: I will not be afraid what man can do unto me.
Thy vows are upon me, O God: I will render praises unto thee.
For thou hast delivered my soul from death: wilt not thou deliver my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of the living?
